title: Your balance
hookLine: worship, work, rest and family: give each its right (Bukhari)

cards: Salman comes to visit his friend Abu al-Darda and finds Abu al-Darda's wife in shabby, careless clothes. What's wrong? he asks. Your brother, she says, has no interest in this world.
Abu al-Darda puts food in front of his guest and says: eat, I'm fasting. Salman says: I won't eat unless you eat. So he eats.
That night Abu al-Darda gets up to pray, and Salman tells him: sleep. Later he gets up again. Sleep, says Salman.
Near the end of the night, Salman wakes him, and the two of them pray together. Then Salman says the line Sahih al-Bukhari keeps.

teach.b: Your Lord has a right over you, your own self has a right over you, and your family has a right over you, so give each one its right.
When they told the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, what had happened, he said: Salman has spoken the truth.

teach.h: A DEVOUT MAN, OUT OF BALANCE.
teach.b: Notice who was out of balance. Not a lazy man. A devout one, fasting through the day and rising to pray through the night, while his wife sat in shabby clothes.
Too much of a good thing had pushed something else out. Another report in Bukhari tells it a second way.

The Prophet hears that the companion Abdullah ibn Amr fasts every day and prays every night, and tells him: fast and break your fast, pray and sleep, for your body has a right over you, your eyes have a right over you, and your wife has a right over you.
Eyes have a right. Sleep isn't a lapse in devotion. It's owed.
Why it holds together: the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." A practice that breaks the person practicing it isn't what was asked.
These weeks you've met a diverse ummah, asked the questions of today, and built a practice for today, one piece at a time. Balance is what keeps all of it standing. Not everything every day.

how: Muslims cite the hadith of Salman and Abu al-Darda, 'give each one its right', as a guide to balancing worship, work, rest and family, so that devotion does not crowd out sleep, health or the rights of a spouse and children.

o: giving Lord, self, family and work each their right
doing as much worship as possible, with no limit
dividing your hours exactly equally among duties

p: told his friend to eat and sleep
fasting by day, rising to pray by night
what Allah asks of a soul

s: the more you fast and pray, the better, with no limit
the Prophet told Abdullah ibn Amr to fast and break his fast, pray and sleep (Sahih al-Bukhari).
the Prophet said Salman had spoken the truth
when told that Salman said 'give each one its right', he agreed (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sleep is a lapse in devotion
in the hadith, your body and your eyes have a right over you.

games.q: you're Salman, visiting your friend. he's fasting, he keeps rising to pray through the night, and his wife is in shabby clothes. what do you do?
o: praise his devotion and leave him to it.
tell him to eat and sleep, and give each one its right.
games.why: Salman made him eat, told him to sleep, prayed with him near the end of the night, and said give each one its right. the Prophet said Salman had spoken the truth (Sahih al-Bukhari).

practice: Go through the four rights one at a time and give each a breath: worship, where it has a place in your day; work, what it asked of you today; family, one face, one need; and yourself, your body, your eyes, how tired they are.
Notice which one got crowded out this week, no blame, just notice. If you pray, thank Allah for the day in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Your balance. Giving your Lord, yourself, your family and your work each their right, so none crowds out the rest. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a right, something owed; also truth.

carryVoice: Your line: give each its right. This block ends here, and the year starts gathering itself in. Rest well tonight.

sources.q: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.
